summary:
A robotic lander near the Moon's south pole needs two things at the same time: sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for radio contact. Both come and go as the Sun and Earth skim the horizon behind mountains and crater rims, so choosing where and when to land is hard to picture from tables of numbers.

Stargazer turns NASA data into something you can see and compare. Using NASA/JPL Horizons positions and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter's LOLA terrain model, it shows when the Sun and Earth are in view from three candidate landing sites (Malapert Massif, the Shackleton rim ridge and Mons Mouton) across four lunar days. Users can stand on the surface in 3D and watch the sky move, compare sites and dates side by side with a simple cost estimate, or learn the ideas by flying a mission game.

The result is a planning aid for mission teams and a way for students and the public to understand why the date matters as much as the site.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Stargazer answers one question for a lunar south pole mission: from this site, on this date, when can a lander see both the Sun and the Earth? It has three parts, reached from one home page.

1. Explore. A 3D view from the surface of each site. The ground and skyline are built from real NASA elevation data, and the Sun and Earth move across the sky as you scrub through time. A status line tells you plainly whether the lander has power, radio contact, both or neither, and when that will next change. A free-fly mode lets you look around the terrain.

2. Plan. A side-by-side comparison of the three sites for each of four lunar days (December 2026 to March 2027). For each site it shows timelines of Sun, Earth and both together, the longest unbroken stretch with both, and plain-language takeaways generated from the numbers. For example, in the first lunar day Malapert Massif has the longest unbroken Sun-and-Earth window at about 384 hours (16 days), but the ranking changes in later lunar days, which shows that the date matters as much as the site.

3. Game. A mission simulator for students and the public. The player finds each site's operating window from the real visibility data, picks a site, assembles a rocket, works a launch pad by hand, clears the flight corridor and launches. The planning stage uses the real data; the launch and flight stages are clearly labelled as simplified gameplay.

HOW IT WORKS

- Sun and Earth directions come from NASA/JPL Horizons as hourly tables for each site.

- The terrain skyline around each site is computed from the LOLA elevation model (80 m per pixel). A body counts as visible only when it is above that skyline, not just above a flat horizon.

- From these we derive visibility windows, per-lunar-day summaries and the longest joint window for every site.

- A Monte Carlo cost model (10,000 trials) estimates cost per usable hour for each site. It is anchored on three published NASA CLPS award values and reports a median with a P10 to P90 range instead of a single figure.

- The results are stored in a database and served by our own API. The website reads live from the API and falls back to a saved copy if the API is unreachable, so it always shows data.

BENEFITS

- Mission planners can compare sites and dates quickly, with terrain taken into account.

- Students and the public can see, not just read, why the lunar south pole is difficult.

- Every number is traceable: the site lists its data sources and marks any value that does not yet have a recorded source.

HONEST LIMITS

Visibility here is geometric line of sight. It does not guarantee electrical power or a working communications link. The cost model is a simplified estimate for comparison, not a mission budget. Surface detail finer than 80 m is illustrative. This is an education and planning prototype, not flight software.

TECHNOLOGIES

Frontend: React, Vite, three.js, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, hosted on Vercel.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL on Neon, hosted on Render.

Data: NASA/JPL Horizons, NASA LRO LOLA LDEM_80S_80M.
